items.title: Mary I burned around 280 Protestants
items.claim: Mary I's reign (1553-1558) earned the 'Bloody Mary' epithet through executions. How many died?

options.text: Around 10,000 — comparable to Henry VIII's executions
Around 280 Protestants burned at the stake, plus 30 who died in prison — a smaller toll than Henry VIII's or Elizabeth I's overall execution numbers
Over 50,000 in a state campaign of terror
No confirmed executions for religion — the epithet is entirely myth

items.reveal:
John Foxe's 'Actes and Monuments' (1563, later 'Foxe's Book of Martyrs') chronicled the Marian burnings in vivid detail and became a foundational Protestant text. Henry VIII executed an estimated 57,000 (Holinshed's figure, contested) including thousands of vagrants; Elizabeth I executed around 200 Catholic priests and Jesuits.

Mary's numbers were lower in absolute terms but concentrated (1555-1558) and ideological. The propaganda effect outlasted the regime.
items.why: Reputation is unevenly distributed. Mary's image as uniquely cruel says more about the durability of Protestant propaganda than about Tudor execution rates.

items.title: One Soviet officer's veto prevented nuclear war in 1962
items.claim: On 27 October 1962, a Soviet submarine (B-59) near Cuba was being depth-charged by the US Navy. The captain ordered a nuclear torpedo prepared for launch. Why didn't it fire?

options.text: Launch required the unanimous consent of three officers; Second Captain Vasily Arkhipov refused
Kennedy's blockade orders explicitly forbade depth-charging Soviet submarines
The submarine surfaced before the launch could be authorised

items.reveal_title: The man who saved the world
items.reveal:
B-59 had been submerged for days, the air was foul, the crew thought war had begun. Captain Valentin Savitsky and political officer Ivan Maslennikov voted to fire. Arkhipov, brigade chief of staff and equal in rank, refused.

Under Soviet protocol, all three had to agree. Arkhipov persuaded Savitsky to surface and await orders. The story only emerged publicly in 2002 at a conference marking the crisis's 40th anniversary; Thomas Blanton of the National Security Archive said 'a guy called Vasily Arkhipov saved the world.'
items.why: Macro-historical narratives about MAD (mutually assured destruction) keeping the peace miss that systems are only as safe as the individuals inside them. Nuclear war was a vote away.

items.title: Lenin tried to remove Stalin from his deathbed
items.claim: In late 1922 and early 1923, Lenin dictated a 'Testament' commenting on his potential successors. What did it say about Stalin?

options.text: It praised Stalin as the most capable administrator and probable successor
It called Stalin 'too rude' and proposed removing him from his post as General Secretary
It did not mention Stalin at all
It endorsed Stalin only as a temporary compromise with Trotsky

items.reveal_title: Suppressed by the man it condemned
items.reveal:
In a postscript dictated on 4 January 1923, Lenin wrote: 'Stalin is too rude and this defect... becomes intolerable in a Secretary-General. That is why I suggest that the comrades think about a way of removing Stalin from that post.'

After Lenin's death in January 1924, the Testament was read at the Central Committee but suppressed. Stalin offered to resign at the 13th Congress; the offer was rejected and the document was buried. It was not published in the USSR until 1956 under Khrushchev.
items.why: Stalin's consolidation of power was not authorised by Lenin — it was achieved despite Lenin's explicit, dying objection. The myth of Stalin as Lenin's chosen heir was built later.
